reference.source: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures
clinicalPearls: Presents with low back pain followed by radicular leg pain (sciatica) that typically radiates below the knee in a dermatomal pattern and is worsened by coughing, sneezing, or sitting
Most prolapses occur at L4/5 and L5/S1, affecting the L5 and S1 nerve roots respectively; the level is inferred from the pattern of pain, weakness, sensory loss, and reflex change
A positive straight-leg-raise (or its variants) reproduces radicular pain and supports nerve-root tension from a disc lesion
The great majority settle with conservative management: reassurance, maintained activity, analgesia, and physiotherapy, as most herniations resorb over weeks to months
Cauda equina syndrome from a large central prolapse is a surgical emergency and must be actively excluded in every patient
Imaging (MRI) is reserved for persistent or severe symptoms, progressive neurological deficit, or when surgery is being considered, since asymptomatic disc bulges are common
Surgery (discectomy) is considered for intractable radicular pain unresponsive to conservative care, significant or progressive motor weakness, or cauda equina compression
Isolated back pain without leg symptoms is usually not due to a surgically treatable disc prolapse
reference.pathophysiology: The intervertebral disc comprises a gelatinous nucleus pulposus contained by the fibrous annulus fibrosus. With age and repetitive loading the annulus weakens and fissures, allowing nuclear material to bulge or herniate, usually posterolaterally where the annulus is thinnest and the posterior longitudinal ligament offers least support. The herniated fragment compresses and inflames the traversing or exiting nerve root, producing radicular pain, and inflammatory mediators from the nucleus contribute to root irritation. A large central herniation can compress the cauda equina. Over time herniated material often shrinks through dehydration and resorption, correlating with symptom resolution.
additionalDifferentials: Lumbar spinal stenosis with neurogenic claudication
Cauda equina syndrome from other causes
Spinal infection (discitis, epidural abscess) or vertebral osteomyelitis
Hip osteoarthritis or greater trochanteric pain referring to the leg
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the lumbar spine as the imaging modality of choice when indicated
Detailed neurological examination for the affected root (motor, sensory, reflexes)
Straight-leg-raise and femoral stretch tests to localise root tension
Urgent MRI if cauda equina syndrome is suspected
Inflammatory markers and further imaging if infection or malignancy is a concern
redFlags: SURGICAL EMERGENCY: cauda equina syndrome (saddle anaesthesia, bladder or bowel dysfunction, bilateral leg symptoms) requires urgent MRI and decompression
Progressive or severe motor weakness (e.g. foot drop) indicating significant root compression
Features suggesting infection or malignancy (fever, weight loss, night pain, history of cancer)
New neurological deficit with structural back pain in the presence of trauma or osteoporosis
reference.prognosis: The natural history is favourable, with most patients improving substantially within weeks to a few months as the herniation resorbs; surgery gives faster relief of radicular pain in selected cases but does not clearly improve very long-term outcome, and recurrence or residual back pain can occur.
pitfalls: Failing to screen for and act on cauda equina syndrome
Ordering MRI too early and over-treating incidental disc bulges that do not explain the symptoms
Attributing pure axial back pain to a disc prolapse amenable to discectomy
Prolonged bed rest, which worsens outcomes compared with maintained activity
references: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures
management: Reassure and treat the majority conservatively with maintained activity, simple analgesia and a short course of NSAIDs, and structured physiotherapy, as most prolapses resorb over weeks to months
Use neuropathic analgesics such as amitriptyline or gabapentinoids for persistent radicular leg pain
Consider an epidural or nerve-root corticosteroid injection for refractory sciatica before contemplating surgery
Actively exclude cauda equina syndrome in every patient and arrange urgent MRI with emergency surgical decompression if suspected
Reserve discectomy for persistent or severe radiculopathy, or a progressive motor deficit, after failure of conservative treatment
Restrict MRI to persistent, severe or progressive symptoms or surgical planning, since asymptomatic disc bulges are common
Refer to orthopaedic or spinal surgery for progressive neurological deficit, disabling pain or surgical consideration
